thread.title: Stock Market's Muted Reaction to End of Shutdown Shows Primacy of Earnings

author: Martin Tillier
title: Stock Market's Muted Reaction to End of Shutdown Shows Primacy of Earnings
text:
During earnings season, nothing else seems to matter. Over the last few days, for example, we have learned beyond doubt what the market thinks of this latest, or any, government shutdown. President Trump announced an end to the partial closure of the government in a press conference that started at around 2:15 pm on Friday. Above is the one-minute chart for the S&P 500 around that time.
As you can see, the chart shows that the market fell as the President spoke and never recovered to the pre-announcement level. I guess you could make a case that the temporary nature of the fix was responsible for that, or that some saw it as a worrying capitulation to House Democrats, or some other complex explanation.
That though is to ignore Occam’s Razor, which holds that the simplest explanation is the most likely to be true. The simplest explanation here is that traders couldn’t care less whether the government is open or closed for business.
There are times when that would matter. If there were nothing else to focus on or worry about, such news would presumably be considered important, but in the meat of earnings season, with an unresolved trade dispute with China that is clearly dragging down growth in that country, and a whole host of other things to worry about, the end of the shutdown was greeted by the market with a massive shrug of the shoulders.
Given that, and with all the other worries being what Donald Rumsfeld famously referred to as “known unknowns,” it is reasonable to assume that the focus this week will be on earnings, and there are some big names reporting. Apple on Tuesday, Facebook and Microsoft on Wednesday, and Amazon on Thursday will all be closely watched, but investors should be careful not to read too much into those results.
Each of the companies mentioned has a stock-specific story that will dominate the coverage and dictate the market reaction, and because of that, how these Titans of Tech performed last quarter will essentially tell us nothing about the broader market.
Apple ( AAPL )
Apple is facing a slowdown in iPhone sales. As I said a couple of weeks ago , any bad news around that looked fully priced in at around $150 and If you bought then you are well positioned to hold through earnings. If not, waiting until after the announcement is probably a better strategy now that the stock had bounced somewhat and given the likelihood of at least some bad news.
Facebook ( FB )
If anything, Facebook’s woes are even more well-known than Apple’s, if different in nature. Their problems are largely political and regulatory and relate to the problems revealed in the Cambridge Analytica saga. As we have just seen in the reaction to the end of the shutdown though, the market is not that worried about politics. There is an inherent understanding that these things come and go, and history suggests that once the brouhaha fades, all that matters is whether or not the corporation concerned gets back to making money. Don’t lose sight of the fact that Facebook is very good at doing just that. The recent rally has lifted FB off the lows too, but at nearly a third lower than the July high, it still looks cheap.
Microsoft ( MSFT )
In this case, the stock specific story is a positive one. Microsoft has seen rapid growth in its cloud business that resulted in the stock climbing through most of last year and holding up better than most when things went south in Q4. It has also been one of the leaders of the rally since Christmas, and while that is understandable given their performance, it does temper enthusiasm for a pre-earnings buy. It is the good news that looks priced in here, which makes a big jump on earnings less likely. I still believe that this will be a strong earnings report, and that MSFT is a buy, but there is not much to be lost by waiting until after the release.
Amazon ( AMZN )
In some ways, the most interesting release of the week, but essentially the least relevant. We have seen many times in that past that what Amazon did in the previous quarter, even in the all-important Q4, is not the point when it comes to the pricing of the stock. They are a company that seem able to turn profit on and off at whim, and the stock is priced almost entirely on growth expectations. That makes the reaction to earnings hard to anticipate, so this is another case where waiting until after the dust settles makes the most sense.
With such high-profile tech names reporting this week, earnings will dominate the conversation. All of the stocks mentioned are available at big discounts to where they were in the middle of last year, and all look worth buying at around these levels. Even so, they will be releasing earnings to a market that is predisposed to see the negative, so in most cases a “wait and see” approach is advisable.
